title: Tensor-Product Crystals and Highest-Weight Crystal Uniqueness

items.title: Tensor products of integrable weight modules and of their crystal lattices
items.statement:
Let $M_1,M_2$ be chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $M_1\otimes M_2$ carry the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module structure of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]] given by the coproduct $\Delta E_i=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i$, $\Delta F_i=F_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes F_i$, $\Delta K_h=K_h\otimes K_h$ of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. Then:

(a) **Grading.** $M_1\otimes M_2$ is a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module for $(M_1\otimes M_2)_\mu=\bigoplus_{\mu_1+\mu_2=\mu}(M_1)_{\mu_1}\otimes(M_2)_{\mu_2}$, a direct sum by [[thm-tensor-products-commute-with-arbitrary-direct-sums]].

(b) **Integrability.** If $M_1,M_2$ are integrable then so is $M_1\otimes M_2$: $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every pure tensor, hence on the whole module.

(c) **Finite weights and bounded support.** If in addition every label-weight space of $M_1,M_2$ is finite dimensional and each weight set is contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$, then the same holds for $M_1\otimes M_2$.

(d) **Tensored lattices.** If $(L_1,B_1),(L_2,B_2)$ are crystal bases of $M_1,M_2$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]), then $L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2$ is a free $A_0$-submodule of $M_1\otimes M_2$ generating it over $\mathbb Q(q)$, satisfies $(L_1\otimes L_2)_\mu=\bigoplus_{\mu_1+\mu_2=\mu}(L_1)_{\mu_1}\otimes(L_2)_{\mu_2}$, and $B_1\otimes B_2$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $(L_1\otimes L_2)/q(L_1\otimes L_2)$ compatible with these weight decompositions.

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
(a) $\Delta K_h$ acts on $(M_1)_{\mu_1}\otimes(M_2)_{\mu_2}$ by $q^{\langle\mu_1,h\rangle}q^{\langle\mu_2,h\rangle}=q^{\langle\mu_1+\mu_2,h\rangle}$, and $\Delta E_i$, $\Delta F_i$ shift the bidegree by $\alpha_i$ and $-\alpha_i$; the direct sum over bidegrees is the published compatibility of tensor products with direct sums.

(b) Put $x:=F_i\otimes1$ and $y:=K_i\otimes F_i$; then $yx=q_i^{-2}xy$, so [[lem-q-binomial-expansion-for-q-commuting-elements]] gives $\Delta(F_i)^n=(x+y)^n=\sum_{j=0}^n\gamma_{n,j}F_i^{\,n-j}K_i^{\,j}\otimes F_i^{\,j}$ with $\gamma_{n,j}\in\mathbb Q(q)$ (only finiteness of the sum matters). On $u\otimes v$ choose $A$ with $F_i^Au=F_i^Av=0$; every term with $n>2A$ has $n-j>A$ or $j>A$ and vanishes, so $F_i$ is locally nilpotent on $u\otimes v$. The same argument with $\Delta E_i=E_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes E_i$, using $(1\otimes E_i)(E_i\otimes K_i^{-1})=q_i^{2}(E_i\otimes K_i^{-1})(1\otimes E_i)$, gives local nilpotence of $E_i$; local nilpotence on all pure tensors gives it on every vector.

(c) For fixed $\mu$ the space $(M_1\otimes M_2)_\mu$ is the sum over pairs $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ with $\mu_1+\mu_2=\mu$ and both label spaces nonzero. Writing $\mu_j=\lambda_j-\nu_j$ with $\nu_j\in Q_+$ inside the finitely many cones containing the weight sets, the relation $\nu_1+\nu_2=\lambda_1+\lambda_2-\mu$ has only finitely many solutions, so the sum is finite and each term is finite dimensional. The weight set of $M_1\otimes M_2$ is contained in the sum of the finitely many cones.

(d) $L_1\otimes L_2$ is free, and $\mathbb Q(q)\otimes_{A_0}(L_1\otimes L_2)\cong M_1\otimes M_2$ by the generation hypotheses; the weight decomposition is the tensor product of the direct sum decompositions of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Since $q(L_1\otimes L_2)=qL_1\otimes L_2+L_1\otimes qL_2$, right exactness of the tensor product gives $(L_1\otimes L_2)/q(L_1\otimes L_2)\cong(L_1/qL_1)\otimes_{\mathbb Q}(L_2/qL_2)$, so $B_1\otimes B_2$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis, weight-graded. Only the easy lattice conditions are established here; stability under the crystal operators is the tensor product theorem on this page.

items.title: The tensor product crystal $B_1\otimes B_2$ and its two-case convention
items.statement:
Let $B_1$ and $B_2$ be crystals, meaning the data $(B,wt,\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i,\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i)$ attached to a crystal basis $(L,B)$ of an integrable module by [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]] and [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]: $wt:B\to P$ is the weight function, $\varepsilon_i(b)=\max\{n:\tilde e_i^nb\ne0\}$ and $\varphi_i(b)=\max\{n:\tilde f_i^nb\ne0\}$ are finite, $\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$, and $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ are the partial maps $B\to B\cup\{0\}$ of [[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]].

The **tensor product crystal** $B_1\otimes B_2$ is the following data on $B_1\times B_2$, whose elements are written $b_1\otimes b_2$:

(i) $wt(b_1\otimes b_2):=wt(b_1)+wt(b_2)$;

(ii) $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, and $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2)$;

(iii) $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, and $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2):=b_1\otimes\tilde e_ib_2$ if $\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2)$.

By convention a product is $0$ as soon as the operator applied to the selected factor is $0$; the **left factor is preferred** exactly in the displayed cases, so the assignment is left-to-right, matching the left-to-right order of the module tensor product $M_1\otimes M_2$ under the coproduct of [[thm-the-drinfeld-jimbo-formulas-define-a-hopf-algebra]]. The **equality case** $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ is split: $\tilde e_i$ acts on the first factor while $\tilde f_i$ acts on the second. The asymmetry is not free: with the same strict or non-strict comparison used for both operators the partial-inverse axiom fails, as the counterexample on the companion page records, while the displayed convention is internally consistent by the lemma on this page computing $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ of $B_1\otimes B_2$.

The functions $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ of $B_1\otimes B_2$ are read off from the two-case operators as maximal iterated powers, exactly as in [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]. This definition only fixes combinatorial data and asserts nothing about an arbitrary pair of crystals: it does not claim that every such datum arises from a module tensor product. When $B_1,B_2$ are the crystals of crystal bases of integrable modules, the tensor product theorem later on this page proves that $(L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2,\,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$ with these operators, and only through that theorem are the values finite and nonnegative a priori. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition fixing the data, the left-to-right preference and the equality cases; the two comparisons are those of JKK Theorem 5.2 (printed pp. 20-21). The asymmetry is forced: if $\tilde f_i$ used the non-strict comparison, then at a vertex with $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ it would act on the first factor, while at the image the resulting $\tilde e_i$ would act on the second, so $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i$ would fail to be the identity on existing edges; the companion-page counterexample exhibits this on $V(2)\otimes V(2)$ for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, and the lemma on this page verifies the displayed convention by a finite case check. The remaining content is bookkeeping: $(b_1,b_2)\mapsto b_1\otimes b_2$ is a bijection, weight additivity is declared, and no existence or axiom claim is made here. The comparison with the module tensor product and the identification of $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are the content of the two following items.

items.title: The $i$-string components of a lattice vector and the single surviving component modulo $q$
items.statement:
Let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of an integrable weight module $M$ in the sense of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]], let $i\in I$, $\lambda\in P$ and $u\in L_\lambda$, and let $u=\sum_{n\ge0}F_i^{(n)}u_n$ be the admissible $i$-string decomposition of $u$: the sum is finite, $u_n\in\ker E_i\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$, and $u_n=0$ whenever $n>\langle h_i,\lambda+n\alpha_i\rangle$ ([[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]]). Then:

(a) **Components lie in the lattice.** $u_n\in L\cap M_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ for every $n$.

(b) **Lattice string decomposition.** $L_\lambda=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\tilde f_i^{\,n}\bigl(L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}\cap\ker E_i\bigr)$, the sum being direct because admissible decompositions are unique; equivalently $L=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\tilde f_i^{\,n}(L\cap\ker E_i)$.

(c) **Single surviving component.** If $u+qL=0$ in $L_\lambda/qL_\lambda$, then $u_n\in qL$ for every $n$. If $u+qL\in B_\lambda$, then there is exactly one index $n_0$ with $u_{n_0}\notin qL$, and for it $u_{n_0}+qL\in B_{\lambda+n_0\alpha_i}$, $u\equiv F_i^{(n_0)}u_{n_0}\pmod{qL}$ and $u_{n_0}+qL=\tilde e_i^{\,n_0}(u+qL)$; in particular $n_0=\varepsilon_i(u+qL)$ ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]), and $\tilde e_iu$ and $\tilde f_iu$ are the residues of $F_i^{(n_0-1)}u_{n_0}$ and $F_i^{(n_0+1)}u_{n_0}$.

Everything is a statement about the fixed lattice $L$ and the operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$; no finite-dimensionality, bounded support, uniform nilpotence or choice principle is assumed. Here F_i^(−1)u is interpreted as0, and F_i^(a+1)u=0 for a top of coroot weight a, so the final formulas include both finite-string endpoints.
items.strategy:
Tail sums and the partial-inverse axiom, following Kashiwara's Proposition 2.3.2(ii) with JKK Lemma 4.5(a) and Theorem 4.7(b).

(a) Put $T_n:=\tilde e_i^{\,n}u\in L_{\lambda+n\alpha_i}$ for $n\ge0$: legitimate because $\tilde e_iL\subseteq L$ is axiom (iii) of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]. Since $\tilde e_i$ acts on the string decomposition by $F_i^{(n)}\mapsto F_i^{(n-1)}$ ([[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]]), $T_n=\sum_{k\ge n}F_i^{(k-n)}u_k$ and hence $\tilde f_iT_{n+1}=T_n-u_n$. As $T_n,T_{n+1}\in L$ and $\tilde f_iL\subseteq L$, each $u_n=T_n-\tilde f_iT_{n+1}$ lies in $L$; the weights are those of the string decomposition.

(b) For $u_n\in L\cap\ker E_i$ the string with top $u_n$ satisfies $\tilde f_i^{\,n}u_n=F_i^{(n)}u_n$, so (a) rewrites $u=\sum_n\tilde f_i^{\,n}u_n$ with every $u_n\in L\cap\ker E_i$; conversely every $\tilde f_i^{\,n}(L\cap\ker E_i)$ lies in $L$ by iterated stability. For a relation among the image summands first discard top components of coroot weight a<n, whose nth image is0; the remaining representatives v_n are admissible. A relation $\sum_n\tilde f_i^{\,n}v_n=0$ is then an admissible decomposition of $0$, so all these representatives v_n=0 by the uniqueness half of [[thm-unique-kashiwara-i-string-decomposition]]; the sum is direct.

(c) Induction on the largest index $N$ of a nonzero string component, proving both clauses simultaneously. The zero vector is immediate. If N=0, u=u0 is a top vector and its residue is either0 or the given basis element, proving both assertions. Let $w:=\tilde e_iu=\sum_{n\ge1}F_i^{(n-1)}u_n\in L$, whose largest possible string index is N−1, with components u1,…,uN; thus the induction strictly decreases even if u0=0. If $u+qL=0$ then $w+qL=0$; by the induction hypothesis applied to $w$ all of $u_1,\dots,u_N$ lie in $qL$, and then $u_0=u-\tilde f_iw\in qL$ as well, because $u\in qL$ and $\tilde f_iw=\sum_{n\ge1}\tilde f_i^{\,n}u_n\in qL$ (each $\tilde f_i^{\,n}$ preserves $L$, hence maps $qL$ into $qL$). Now let $u+qL=b\in B_\lambda$; then $w+qL=\tilde e_ib\in B\cup\{0\}$ by axiom (v). If $w+qL=0$, the first clause applied to $w$ gives $u_1,\dots,u_N\in qL$, so $u\equiv u_0\pmod{qL}$ and $u_0+qL=u+qL=b\in B$: the claim with $n_0=0$. If $w+qL\in B$, the induction hypothesis applied to $w$ gives a unique index $n_0\ge1$ with $u_{n_0}\notin qL$, $u_{n_0}+qL\in B$ and $w\equiv F_i^{(n_0-1)}u_{n_0}\pmod{qL}$. Applying the linear operator $\tilde f_i$ (which preserves $L$) gives $\tilde f_iw\equiv F_i^{(n_0)}u_{n_0}\pmod{qL}$. On the other hand $u=u_0+\tilde f_iw$, and $(\tilde f_iw)+qL=\tilde f_i(w+qL)=\tilde f_i\tilde e_ib=b$ by the partial-inverse axiom, so $\tilde f_iw\equiv u\pmod{qL}$; hence $u_0\equiv0\pmod{qL}$, that is $u_0\in qL$, and $u\equiv F_i^{(n_0)}u_{n_0}\pmod{qL}$ with $u_{n_0}+qL=\tilde e_i^{n_0}b\in B$. Uniqueness of $n_0$ follows from $\tilde e_i^{n}b\ne0$ exactly for $n\le\varepsilon_i(b)$ ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]). The final clause is the definition of $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ on the string. Every step involves only finite string data and the stability of $L$; no choice principle occurs.

references.title: Masaki Kashiwara, On crystal bases of the q-analogue of universal enveloping algebras, Duke Math. J. 63 (1991), no. 2, 465-516
references.locator: §2.3, printed pp. 474-475, Proposition 2.3.2(ii): for $u=\sum_{n=0}^Nf_i^{(n)}u_n\in L_\lambda$ all $u_n$ belong to $L$; if $u$ mod $qL$ belongs to $B$ then $u_n\in qL$ for $n\ne n_0$, $u_{n_0}$ mod $qL$ lies in $B$ and $u\equiv f_i^{(n_0)}u_{n_0}$ mod $qL$.

items.title: Highest weight elements, lowering-generated subcrystals and highest weight crystals
items.statement:
Let $B$ be a crystal, meaning the data $(B,wt,\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i,\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i)$ attached to a crystal basis or to a tensor product of such data ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]], [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]]).

A vertex $b\in B$ is a **highest weight element** (a highest vertex, a maximal vector) of weight $\lambda\in P$ if $wt(b)=\lambda$ and $\tilde e_ib=0$ for every $i\in I$. The **lowering-generated subcrystal** of $b$ is
$$F(b):=\{\tilde f_{i_1}\cdots\tilde f_{i_r}b:\ r\ge0,\ i_1,\dots,i_r\in I\}\setminus\{0\},$$
the set of all nonzero iterated lowering images of $b$; it contains $b$ and is closed under every $\tilde f_i$. The **connected component** $C(b)$ of $b$ is the smallest subset of $B$ containing $b$ and closed under $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ for all $i$; by the partial-inverse axiom this is the connected component of the underlying coloured graph.

$B$ is a **highest weight crystal of highest weight $\lambda$** if $B$ has a highest weight element $b$ of weight $\lambda$ and $B=F(b)$.

The definition deliberately separates two conditions. Always $F(b)\subseteq C(b)$, and a highest vertex need not generate $B$: in a tensor product $B_1\otimes B_2$ a vertex with $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\varphi_i(b_1)$ for all $i$ is highest while $B_1\otimes B_2$ is in general larger than its lowering-generated subcrystal (the companion page computes both cases). Conversely, for abstract crystals the two conditions do not determine $B$ up to isomorphism: the source literature records that not every connected crystal with a highest weight element of weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $B(\lambda)$. In this library crystals come from crystal bases of modules, and uniqueness for those is a theorem proved later on this page, not a consequence of this definition.

For the canonical objects, $B(\lambda)=\mathcal B(\lambda)$ denotes the crystal of the simple highest weight module $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ ([[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]]) and $P^+$ the dominant integral labels ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); that $B(\lambda)$ is a highest weight crystal of highest weight $\lambda$ is the next theorem. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: A definition with the two conditions stated separately: $F(b)$ is the closure of $\{b\}$ under the lowering operators alone, while $C(b)$ is its closure under both, the usual graph component. The distinction is not cosmetic: the two-case rule shows that a highest vertex of a tensor product generates one $i$-string colour at a time, so $F(b)$ is usually strictly smaller than the crystal. The abstract-crystal caveat is recorded so that the definition is not read as a uniqueness assertion; components are identified only through the crystal-basis theorems later on this page. No objects are chosen and no basis is selected. The comparison with the canonical $B(\lambda)$ is deferred to the next theorem, which is the first place where existence of a highest weight crystal is asserted.

references.title: Sami Assaf, Anne Dranowski and Nicolle Gonzalez, Extremal tensor products of Demazure crystals, arXiv:2210.10236
references.locator: §2: 'In general, we say an element $b\in B$ is highest weight if $E\{b\}=0$. A connected crystal $B$ is a highest weight crystal with highest weight $\lambda$ if there exists a highest weight element $b_\lambda$ of weight $\lambda$ such that $B=F\{b_\lambda\}$', followed by 'Note not every highest weight crystal with highest weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $B(\lambda)$'.

items.title: The crystal basis of a tensor product and the two-case operator rule
items.statement:
Let $M_1,M_2$ be integrable chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules with crystal bases $(L_1,B_1)$, $(L_2,B_2)$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]), and let $M_1\otimes M_2$ be the integrable module of [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]].

Then $(L_1\otimes_{A_0}L_2,\,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis of $M_1\otimes M_2$, and its crystal is the tensor product crystal $B_1\otimes B_2$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]]: for all $b_1\in B_1$, $b_2\in B_2$ and $i\in I$,
$$\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}\qquad \tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\begin{cases}\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2),\\ b_1\otimes\tilde e_ib_2,&\varphi_i(b_1)<\varepsilon_i(b_2),\end{cases}$$
with value $0$ as soon as the selected factor maps to $0$. In particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$ map $B_1\otimes B_2$ into $(B_1\otimes B_2)\cup\{0\}$, and for all $b,b'\in B_1\otimes B_2$ one has $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$, so the partial-inverse axiom holds. The equality case $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ is resolved as in the definition: $\tilde f_i$ acts on the second factor and $\tilde e_i$ on the first.

No finite dimensionality, bounded support or uniform nilpotence is assumed, and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
Reduction to rank-one $i$-strings, then the local rank-one tensor rule.

1.1 (Lifts with a single component.) Fix $b_1\otimes b_2\in B_1\otimes B_2$ and lifts $u_j\in L_j$ with $u_j+qL_j=b_j$. By [[lem-i-string-components-of-a-crystal-lattice]](c) with $n_j=\varepsilon_i(b_j)$, $u_j\equiv F_i^{(n_j)}w_j\pmod{qL_j}$ for top components $w_j\in L_j\cap\ker E_i$ with $w_j+qL_j=\tilde e_i^{n_j}b_j\in B_j$. Hence $u_1\otimes u_2\equiv h:=F_i^{(n_1)}w_1\otimes F_i^{(n_2)}w_2\pmod{q(L_1\otimes L_2)}$, and $h$ has residue $b_1\otimes b_2$. [construct, step 1.1]

2.1 (The rank-one block.) Let $N_j:=U_iw_j$. As $w_j\in\ker E_i$ and $M_j$ is integrable, $N_j$ is the finite-dimensional rank-one simple with top $w_j$ and divided basis $F_i^{(k)}w_j$, $0\le k\le a_j:=\langle h_i,wt(w_j)\rangle\ge0$, and $F_i^{(k)}w_j=\tilde f_i^{\,k}w_j\in L_j$ for all $k$ by [[lem-i-string-components-of-a-crystal-lattice]](b). The injection $N_1\otimes N_2\to M_1\otimes M_2$ is $U_i$-linear, and the string operators of $M_1\otimes M_2$ restrict to the image because string components of a vector in a $U_i$-submodule again lie in it, by uniqueness of admissible decompositions. [step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Apply [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]] to the pair $(w_1,w_2)$ with divided bases $v_j=F_i^{(j)}w_1$, $w_k=F_i^{(k)}w_2$ and its $A_0$-tensor lattice. That lemma is a finite, choice-free computation, and it gives, modulo $q$ times its tensor lattice, $\tilde f_i(v_{n_1}\otimes w_{n_2})=v_{n_1+1}\otimes w_{n_2}$ if $a_1-n_1>n_2$ and $v_{n_1}\otimes w_{n_2+1}$ otherwise, while $\tilde e_i$ acts on the first factor if $a_1-n_1\ge n_2$ and on the second otherwise. [step 2.1]

3.1 (Transport to the module tensor product.) The injection commutes with $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$, so the congruences of step 2.2 hold modulo $q(L_1\otimes L_2)$ for $h$. Since $\varphi_i(b_1)=a_1-n_1$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)=n_2$ by step 1.1, the two cases are exactly those displayed in the statement; the residue of $F_i^{(n_1+1)}w_1\otimes F_i^{(n_2)}w_2$ is $\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2$ because $\tilde f_iF_i^{(n_1)}w_1=F_i^{(n_1+1)}w_1$ and residues are transported along the string by [[lem-i-string-components-of-a-crystal-lattice]](c), and similarly for the second factor. [step 2.2, step 1.1]

4.1 (Stability before taking residues.) For arbitrary weight vectors u_j∈L_j use the FULL decomposition from lem-i-string-components-of-a-crystal-lattice(a),(b), not just a chosen leading residue: each u_j is a finite sum F_i^(n)w_(j,n) with w_(j,n)∈L_j∩ker E_i. Every pair of nonzero tops generates a finite rank-one block with divided bases lying in L_j. The rank-one tensor supplier proves exact preservation of that block's A0 tensor lattice by both string operators. Its U_i-linear inclusion commutes with those operators. Thus each term of the finite expanded pure tensor has its images in L1⊗L2, and linearity proves stability for arbitrary lattice vectors. Now the congruences from steps1.1–3.1 may be transported to arbitrary lifts, because operators preserve q(L1⊗L2). The grading/generation/residue-basis axioms are the integrability lemma(a),(d); the operator-basis axiom is the established congruence. No stability of a q-error is assumed before it is proved. [step 2.2, step 2.1, step 1.1]

5.1 (Partial inverse.) If $\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ and $\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=b'$, then $\varphi_i(\tilde f_ib_1)=\varphi_i(b_1)-1\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, so $\tilde e_i$ selects the first factor at $b'$ and $\tilde e_ib'=\tilde e_i\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2=b_1\otimes b_2$ by the one-factor partial-inverse axiom. If $\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, then, when the image b′ is nonzero, $\tilde f_ib_2\ne0$ and $\varepsilon_i(\tilde f_ib_2)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)+1>\varphi_i(b_1)$, so $\tilde e_i$ selects the second factor and returns $b$. The converse implication is the same computation read backwards, and it uses exactly the split equality cases of the definition: at $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ both consistency conditions hold simultaneously. Hence $(L_1\otimes L_2,B_1\otimes B_2)$ is a crystal basis whose crystal is $B_1\otimes B_2$. [step 4.1, given]

6.1 Every step above used only finite string data, the two one-factor crystal bases and the published lattice facts; no basis of an infinite-dimensional space is chosen. [step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

items.title: The weight, $\varepsilon_i$ and $\varphi_i$ formulas for the tensor product crystal
items.strategy:
Finite case analysis on the two integer pairs, following the definitions.

(a) is the declared weight of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]], inherited from the module tensor product.

(b),(d) Write p=phi_i(b1), a=epsilon_i(b1), s=epsilon_i(b2), r=phi_i(b2). Under e_i on the first factor p INCREASES by1 and a decreases by1; on the second s decreases by1. If p≥s initially, all a raising steps use the first factor and then stop, so epsilon=a. If p<s, first s−p raising steps use the second, reaching the tie, and then a steps use the first, so epsilon=a+s−p. These steps exist because s−p≤s and a≥0. Hence epsilon=a+max(0,s−p)=max(a,s−p+a). The first maximum entry is attained for p≥s, including equality, whereas f chooses the first only for p>s: the maximum equality alone cannot determine the strict branch. For f, if p>s it first uses p−s lowering steps on the first factor, reaches equality, then uses r steps on the second; if p≤s it uses r steps on the second. Thus phi=r+max(0,p−s). This proves the branch assertions with their correct tie qualifications.

(c) Using (b) and $\varphi=\varepsilon+\langle h_i,wt\rangle$: $\varphi_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\max(a,s-p+a)+(p-a)+(r-s)=\max(p+r-s,r)=\max\bigl(\varphi_i(b_1)+\langle h_i,wt(b_2)\rangle,\varphi_i(b_2)\bigr)$.

(e) Suppose $\varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ and $b=\tilde f_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2$; then $\varphi_i(\tilde f_ib_1)=\varphi_i(b_1)-1\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ by the strict inequality, so by (d) the $\tilde e_i$-rule selects the first factor at $b'$ and $\tilde e_ib'=\tilde e_i\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2=b_1\otimes b_2$ by the one-factor partial-inverse axiom. Suppose $\varphi_i(b_1)\le\varepsilon_i(b_2)$ and $b'=b_1\otimes\tilde f_ib_2$; then, assuming the displayed image b′ is nonzero, $\tilde f_ib_2\ne0$ and $\varepsilon_i(\tilde f_ib_2)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)+1>\varphi_i(b_1)$, so $\tilde e_i$ selects the second factor and returns $b$. The converse direction is the same computation read backwards. With any other placement of the equality cases the identity $\tilde e_i\tilde f_i=\mathrm{id}$ on existing edges fails at a vertex with $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)\ne0$, which is the abstract form of the counterexample on the companion page.

(f) Iterating (d): $\tilde f_i$ keeps acting on the same factor as long as its case persists, and each application increases $\varepsilon_i$ by one and decreases $\varphi_i$ by one, by the crystal axioms of the factors and (b),(c). All steps are finite checks on two fixed integers.

items.title: The dual crystal: reversed arrows, negated weights and swapped $\varepsilon/\varphi$
items.statement:
Let $B$ be the crystal of a crystal basis $(L,B)$ of an integrable module ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]], [[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]); its operators are the partial maps $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i:B\to B\cup\{0\}$ satisfying $\tilde e_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde f_ib'$, and $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ satisfy $\varphi_i(b)-\varepsilon_i(b)=\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$.

Define the **dual crystal** $B^\vee:=\{b^\vee:b\in B\}$ by
$$wt(b^\vee):=-wt(b),\qquad \varepsilon_i(b^\vee):=\varphi_i(b),\qquad \varphi_i(b^\vee):=\varepsilon_i(b),\qquad \tilde f_i(b^\vee):=(\tilde e_ib)^\vee,\qquad \tilde e_i(b^\vee):=(\tilde f_ib)^\vee,$$
with $0^\vee:=0$. Then:

(i) $B^\vee$ satisfies the crystal axioms: $(\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i)$ are partial inverses, the arrows of $B^\vee$ are the arrows of $B$ with orientation reversed, the displayed $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are exactly the maximal iterated powers, and $(B^\vee)^\vee=B$ canonically;

(ii) **tensor products reverse order.** For crystals $B_1,B_2$ as above the map $b_1\otimes b_2\mapsto b_2^\vee\otimes b_1^\vee$ is an isomorphism of crystals $(B_1\otimes B_2)^\vee\to B_2^\vee\otimes B_1^\vee$ for the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]].

The construction is stated for crystals of crystal bases of integrable modules, where $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are finite and nonnegative. For the negative-half crystal of [[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]] only the formal $\varphi_i=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,wt\rangle$, which may be negative, is defined, and no dual is asserted there. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
A finite verification from the axioms.

(i) Partial inverses: $\tilde f_i(b^\vee)=b'^\vee$ iff $\tilde e_ib=b'$ iff $b=\tilde f_ib'$ iff $b^\vee=\tilde e_i(b'^\vee)$, which is exactly the required equivalence. Arrows: $b\to b'$ in $B$ means $\tilde f_ib=b'$, and in $B^\vee$ one has $\tilde f_i(b'^\vee)=(\tilde e_ib')^\vee=b^\vee$, so the arrow runs from $b'^\vee$ to $b^\vee$; the orientation is reversed. Maximal iterated powers: $\max\{n:\tilde e_i^n(b^\vee)\ne0\}=\max\{n:\tilde f_i^nb\ne0\}=\varphi_i(b)$ and $\max\{n:\tilde f_i^n(b^\vee)\ne0\}=\varepsilon_i(b)$. Weight pairing: $\varphi_i(b^\vee)-\varepsilon_i(b^\vee)=\varepsilon_i(b)-\varphi_i(b)=-\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle=\langle h_i,wt(b^\vee)\rangle$. Involutivity is immediate from the definition.

(ii) Let S((b1⊗b2)^vee)=b2^vee⊗b1^vee. Set p=phi_i(b1), s=epsilon_i(b2). The f operator on the dual input corresponds to e on b1⊗b2. If p≥s, e acts on b1 and its image under S is b2^vee⊗(e_i b1)^vee=b2^vee⊗f_i(b1^vee). On the target the f rule selects its second factor precisely because phi_i(b2^vee)=s≤p=epsilon_i(b1^vee). If p<s, e acts on b2 and S gives f_i(b2^vee)⊗b1^vee; the target f rule selects its first factor because s>p. The e calculation corresponds to original f: p>s gives the target second factor since s<p, and p≤s gives the target first since s≥p. Zero endpoints agree. The target weight is −wt(b1)−wt(b2), the weight of the dual input; the maximal string lengths therefore agree. This proves the crystal isomorphism with exactly the required tie cases.

items.title: Uniqueness: crystal bases of integrable modules decompose into highest weight crystals
items.statement:
**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).

(i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.

(ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.

(iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

**Choice.** The axiom of choice is declared in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used to obtain the decomposition of $M$ into simple integrable highest weight modules from [[prop-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-modules-are-semisimple]], which selects bases of the finite-dimensional maximal-vector spaces simultaneously. It also permits simultaneous choices of lifts of the finite residue bases in the possibly infinite family of top spaces. After those choices, each lattice and crystal argument is finite and choice-free. No incompatible-axiom branch is used, and no global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness is assumed. The index set J need not be finite in affine or indefinite type; local weight finiteness means only finitely many summands contribute to any fixed label-weight space.
items.strategy:
Kashiwara's proof of Theorem 3 in §2.6, transported to the library's conventions, with [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]](iii) playing the role of his Lemma 2.6.1(i).

Step A (structure of the top isotypic part). Each nonzero $w\in M_\lambda$ generates a nonzero integrable cyclic highest weight module of weight $\lambda$, which is $V(\lambda)$ by the universality in [[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]; the sum $N_0=U_qM_\lambda$ of these submodules is the $V(\lambda)$-isotypic component, hence $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$, and $N_1$, the sum of the other isotypic components, is a $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-submodule with $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and no weight $\lambda$ (if lambda is a weight of V(nu), then nu≥lambda is a nonzero weight of M, so maximality of lambda forces nu=lambda).

Step B (descent for $V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$). Choose lifts in L_lambda of the finite residue basis B_lambda. Their determinant is a q0 unit, so they are an A0-basis; send each lift to the top vector in its own V(lambda) copy. This fixes the top residue basis, not merely the top lattice. Claim: if $u\in V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}_\mu$ with $\mu\ne\lambda$ and $\tilde e_iu\in\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ for all $i$, then $u\in\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$. Take the minimal $n\ge0$ with $q^nu\in\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$; if $n>0$ then $b:=q^nu+q\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}\ne0$ is homogeneous of weight $\mu$ and killed by every $\tilde e_i$, since $\tilde e_i(q^nu)=q^n\tilde e_iu\in q^n\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}\subseteq q\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$. Writing $b=\sum_jb^{(j)}$ componentwise, each $b^{(j)}$ is killed by every $\tilde e_i$, so each $b^{(j)}=0$ by [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]](iii) (note $\mu\ne\lambda$); hence $b=0$, a contradiction.

Step C ($L\cap N_0$ is standard). $L_0:=L\cap N_0$ is a crystal lattice of $N_0$: it is weight-graded, stable under $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$, and generates N0 because its top lattice L_lambda spans M_lambda and lowering words generate U_q M_lambda. Hence $\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}\subseteq L_0$ (it is generated by the $\tilde f_i$-words applied to $(L_0)_\lambda$), and $L_0\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ by descending induction on $\operatorname{ht}(\lambda-\mu)$: for $u\in(L_0)_\mu$ with $\mu\ne\lambda$ every $\tilde e_iu\in(L_0)_{\mu+\alpha_i}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ by induction, so Step B applies, while at $\mu=\lambda$ we have equality of top parts by construction. Thus $L_0=\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$.

Step D (splitting). Weights mu outside lambda−Q_+ have zero N0 component and split trivially; within that cone the following finite-height induction applies. For $u\in L_\mu$ write $u=u_0+u_1$ with $u_j\in N_j$. Descending induction on $\operatorname{ht}(\lambda-\mu)$: at $\mu=\lambda$ we have $u_1=0$ because $N_1$ has no weight $\lambda$; for $\mu\ne\lambda$, $\tilde e_iu\in L_{\mu+\alpha_i}$ has smaller height, so by induction its $N_0$-component $\tilde e_iu_0$ lies in $L_0=\mathcal L(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ (the operators preserve each $N_j$), and Step B gives $u_0\in L_0$; then $u_1=u-u_0\in L\cap N_1$. This proves $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$; note that no descent statement for $N_1$ is needed. The two summands are crystal lattices of $N_0,N_1$.

Step E (the residue basis splits). $B_0:=B\cap(L_0/qL_0)$ is linearly independent and stable under $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ by stability of $L_0$, weight-graded, and contains the $m$ top residues; Step F below identifies it with the standard residue basis up to scalars and thereby shows that it spans $L_0/qL_0$. In the remaining part of this step only $B_0\subseteq B$ is used. For $b\in B\setminus B_0$, write $b=b_0+b_1$ in $L/qL=L_0/qL_0\oplus L_1/qL_1$ and suppose $b_0\ne0$; then either $\mu\ne\lambda$ and some $\tilde e_i$ survives on $b_0$ by [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]](iii), so $\tilde e_ib\ne0$ and, by descending induction on the height, $\tilde e_ib\in B_0$ (its $N_1$-component vanishes), whence $b=\tilde f_i\tilde e_ib\in L_0/qL_0\cap B=B_0$ by the partial-inverse axiom, a contradiction; or $\mu=\lambda$ and $b_0\ne0$ is a combination of top residues, so $b\in B_\lambda=B_{0,\lambda}$ because $\#B_\lambda=\dim M_\lambda=m=\#B_{0,\lambda}$. Hence $B=B_0\sqcup B_1$ with $B_1:=B\setminus B_0\subseteq L_1/qL_1$, and counting dimensions weight by weight shows that $B_1$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $L_1/qL_1$.

Step F (identification up to scalars). B0 is the stable subset of B containing all chosen top residues. Step C and the field U-isomorphism identify each chosen top with the top of its own canonical copy. Lowering-word generation identifies B0 with the full standard residue basis and therefore proves it spans and is a crystal basis; no spanning premise is assumed here. In particular its residue basis has exactly one element in each top weight space of the m copies; writing it as $\alpha_j\,b_\lambda^{(j)}$ in the $j$-th copy and using that every vertex of $\mathcal B(\lambda)$ is a lowering word from $b_\lambda$ ([[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]](ii)), induction along lowering words shows $B_0=\bigsqcup_j\alpha_j\,\mathcal B(\lambda)^{(j)}$; the scalars are removed by composing the identification with the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-automorphism of $V(\lambda)$ multiplying the highest vector by $\alpha_j^{-1}$ (the top weight space is one dimensional, so this is an automorphism).

Step G (locally finite iteration). Do not assert there are finitely many simple constituents: in affine type, dominant labels lambda−n delta can occur for arbitrarily large n. For any fixed label mu, the set of possible nonzero weights nu≥mu is finite: support lies in finitely many cones lambda_a−Q_+, and nu=mu+gamma=lambda_a−beta requires gamma+beta=lambda_a−mu, whose nonnegative simple-root coefficients give finitely many possibilities. This uses the chosen grading and independent simple roots. Thus one can peel maximal top isotypic components in increasing distance from the finite upper cone bounds; there are finitely many tops at each height and finite multiplicity at each top. Each fixed weight is exhausted after finitely many such removals, so the successive split lattices and residue bases define actual direct sums, not infinite completed sums or a limiting lattice. Equivalently apply the initial semisimple decomposition and the top-splitting lemma locally in that finite upper interval. The projections and identifications are compatible as the interval enlarges because an isotypic component and its standard lattice are fixed after it is split. Choose the top basis lifts in each component as in Step B; any simultaneous choice needed is covered by the declared axiom of choice. This yields Phi, equality of lattices and crystal bases for a possibly infinite locally weight-finite J. Clause(iii) follows componentwise from the canonical highest crystal theorem. No global Laurent freeness or integral splitting is used.

items.title: Highest weight components in a tensor product crystal
items.statement:
**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), inherited through [[thm-crystal-bases-of-integrable-modules-decompose-into-highest-weight-crystals]]. Let $M_1,M_2$ be integrable chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight modules with finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight sets contained in finite unions of cones, let $(L_1,B_1),(L_2,B_2)$ be crystal bases of $M_1,M_2$, and let $B_1\otimes B_2$ be the crystal of $M_1\otimes M_2$ ([[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]], [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]]).

(a) **Highest vertices.** For $b=b_1\otimes b_2\in B_1\otimes B_2$ the following are equivalent: (i) $b$ is a highest weight element, i.e. $\tilde e_ib=0$ for every $i\in I$; (ii) $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle$ for every $i\in I$; (iii) $\varepsilon_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=0$ for every $i\in I$. In this case $wt(b)=wt(b_1)+wt(b_2)$ is dominant.

(b) **Generated components.** For every highest vertex $b\in B_1\otimes B_2$ of weight $\lambda$, the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ is a connected component of $B_1\otimes B_2$, is isomorphic as a crystal to the canonical $B(\lambda)=\mathcal B(\lambda)$ of [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]], and $\lambda\in P^+$.

(c) **Decomposition.** $B_1\otimes B_2$ is the disjoint union of the subcrystals $F(b)$ over the highest weight elements $b\in B_1\otimes B_2$, each of which is a highest weight crystal in the sense of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]; the multiplicity of $B(\lambda)$ as a component equals the multiplicity of $V(\lambda)$ in the tensor product module $M_1\otimes M_2$.

No choice principle beyond the inherited one is used.
items.strategy:
(a) By [[lem-crystal-tensor-product-weight-epsilon-and-phi-formulas]](b), $\varepsilon_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=\max(\varepsilon_i(b_1),\varepsilon_i(b_2)-\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle)$, so $\tilde e_i(b_1\otimes b_2)=0$ for all $i$ if and only if this maximum is $0$ for all $i$, i.e. $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle$; this is the equivalence of (i),(ii) and, by definition, of (iii). Dominance: $\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle=\varphi_i(b)\ge0$ because $\varepsilon_i(b)=0$ and $\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$ is finite and nonnegative for a crystal of an integrable module ([[def-crystal-graph-epsilon-phi-and-weight]]).

(b) Apply [[thm-crystal-bases-of-integrable-modules-decompose-into-highest-weight-crystals]] to $M_1\otimes M_2$, which satisfies the category hypotheses by [[lem-tensor-products-of-integrable-weight-modules-are-integrable]](a)-(c), with the crystal basis $(L_1\otimes L_2,B_1\otimes B_2)$ of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. The theorem decomposes the crystal into components $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ whose highest vertices are exactly the highest weight elements (clause (iii)). The component of $b$ therefore is a highest weight crystal of weight $\lambda=wt(b)$; by [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]](ii) its vertex set is $F(b)$, and its identification with $\mathcal B(\lambda)$ is the transported isomorphism of the uniqueness theorem.

(c) The disjoint-union statement is the component decomposition of the same theorem together with the uniqueness of the highest vertex in each component; the multiplicity statement is clause (ii) there applied to $M_1\otimes M_2$, whose highest weight multiplicities are those of the tensor product module. The axiom of choice is used only through the uniqueness theorem, where it is already declared; no new nonconstructive step occurs.

title: Tensor-Product Crystals and Highest-Weight Crystal Uniqueness — Examples

items.title: Changing the equality case in the tensor rule breaks the partial-inverse axiom
items.statement:
Claim refuted: on the product of two crystals the two operators may be defined by the same kind of comparison, namely
$$\tilde f_i^{\prime}(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2\ \text{ if }\ \varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2),\qquad \tilde e_i^{\prime}(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2\ \text{ if }\ \varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2),$$
with the second factor used in the remaining cases and $0$ whenever the selected factor maps to $0$; that is, the two equality cases of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] are exchanged.

Counterexample: take $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, the rank-one simples of highest weights $a=b=2$ with divided bases $v_j=F_1^{(j)}v_0,\ w_k=F_1^{(k)}w_0$, and the vertex $b=v_1\otimes w_1$. Then $\varphi_1(v_1)=1=\varepsilon_1(w_1)$, so the modified rule uses the non-strict comparison and acts on the first factor: $\tilde f_1^{\prime}(v_1\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_1$. At the image $b'=v_2\otimes w_1$ one has $\varphi_1(v_2)=0\le\varepsilon_1(w_1)=1$, and the modified $\tilde e_1^{\prime}$ acts on the first factor only when $\varphi_1>\varepsilon_1$, so it acts on the second factor: $\tilde e_1^{\prime}(v_2\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_0\ne v_1\otimes w_1$. Hence $\tilde f_1^{\prime}b=b'$ while $\tilde e_1^{\prime}b'\ne b$: the partial-inverse axiom fails, so $(B(a)\otimes B(b),\tilde e^{\prime},\tilde f^{\prime})$ is not a crystal, and a fortiori not the crystal $B(a)\otimes B(b)$ of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. The same failure occurs if one uses the strict comparison for both operators, or the non-strict comparison for both; by contrast the rank-one computation of [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]] shows that with the convention of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] the string through $v_0\otimes w_1$ is $v_0\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_2$ of length three, whereas the modified rule produces the four-element chain $v_0\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_1,v_2\otimes w_1,v_2\otimes w_2$, so the modified graph has the wrong component size and cannot be the crystal of $V(2)\otimes V(2)=V(4)\oplus V(2)\oplus V(0)$.
items.strategy:
A finite computation at the boundary case $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, following the rank-one analysis of [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]].

1.1 Set $a=b=2$ and index the divided bases by their string positions, so that $\varphi_1(v_j)=2-j=\varepsilon_1(v_j)$ reversed: $\varepsilon_1(v_j)=j$ and $\varphi_1(v_j)=2-j$, and similarly for $w_k$. The vertex $v_1\otimes w_1$ satisfies $\varphi_1(v_1)=1=\varepsilon_1(w_1)=1$; this is the equality case in which the two conventions differ. [given, algebra]

2.1 Under the modified rule $\tilde f_1^{\prime}$ acts on the first factor at this vertex, because it uses $\varphi_1\ge\varepsilon_1$: $\tilde f_1^{\prime}(v_1\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_1$. [step 1.1]

2.2 At $v_2\otimes w_1$ one has $\varphi_1(v_2)=0$ and $\varepsilon_1(w_1)=1$, so both the modified and the original rule select a factor by the comparison of $0$ with $1$; the modified $\tilde e_1^{\prime}$ acts on the first factor only when $\varphi_1>\varepsilon_1$, which fails, so it acts on the second: $\tilde e_1^{\prime}(v_2\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_0$. [step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Therefore $\tilde e_1^{\prime}\tilde f_1^{\prime}(v_1\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_0\ne v_1\otimes w_1$, contradicting the partial-inverse axiom of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]] that every crystal satisfies, so the modified data is not a crystal; the same computation with both comparisons strict fails at $\varphi_1=\varepsilon_1+1$, and with both non-strict at a vertex with $\varphi_1=\varepsilon_1$. [step 2.2, step 1.1]

4.1 Compare component sizes: the original rank-one tensor rule of [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]] gives $\tilde f_1(v_j\otimes w_k)=v_{j+1}\otimes w_k$ if $2-j>k$ and $v_j\otimes w_{k+1}$ otherwise; through $v_0\otimes w_1$ this is $v_0\otimes w_1\to v_1\otimes w_1\to v_1\otimes w_2$, a chain of three, which is $B(2)$ in the component decomposition of $V(2)\otimes V(2)=V(4)\oplus V(2)\oplus V(0)$. The modified rule instead produces $v_0\otimes w_1\to v_1\otimes w_1\to v_2\otimes w_1\to v_2\otimes w_2\to0$, a chain of four, which is not a component of the crystal of any module in the decomposition. [step 3.1, given]

5.1 Consequently the equality case in [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] is not a matter of taste: the assignment $\tilde f_i$ strict and $\tilde e_i$ non-strict is the one for which the partial-inverse axiom and the component sizes of the rank-one computation agree, and the alternative conventions produce different coloured graphs with a different number of vertices in the affected string. [step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

items.title: The tensor crystal $B(1)\otimes B(1)$ for $\mathfrak{sl}_2$
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, $I=\{1\}$, with fundamental weight $\lambda_1$ and simple root $\alpha_1=2\lambda_1$. Let $V(1)$ be the two-dimensional simple integrable module with highest vector $v_0$ and crystal $B(1)=\{v_0,v_1\}$, where $v_1=F_1v_0$; the $i$-string is $v_0\xrightarrow{1}v_1$ with $wt(v_0)=\lambda_1$, $wt(v_1)=-\lambda_1$ and $\varepsilon_1(v_0)=0,\ \varphi_1(v_0)=1,\ \varepsilon_1(v_1)=1,\ \varphi_1(v_1)=0$ (JKK Example 5.1(a) with $m=1$).

Compute the tensor crystal $B(1)\otimes B(1)$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] with the two-case rule of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. Writing the four vertices as $v_j\otimes v_k$ with $j,k\in\{0,1\}$, the rule gives
$$\tilde f_1(v_j\otimes v_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j+1}\otimes v_k,&1-j>k,\\ v_j\otimes v_{k+1},&1-j\le k,\end{cases}\qquad \tilde e_1(v_j\otimes v_k)=\begin{cases}v_{j-1}\otimes v_k,&1-j\ge k,\\ v_j\otimes v_{k-1},&1-j<k.\end{cases}$$
Consequently: $v_0\otimes v_0$ is the unique highest vertex of weight $2\lambda_1$ and generates the chain $v_0\otimes v_0\to v_1\otimes v_0\to v_1\otimes v_1$; the remaining vertex $v_0\otimes v_1$ has weight $0$, is killed by $\tilde e_1$ and by $\tilde f_1$, and forms a one-element component; and $\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1$ of the four vertices are $(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(0,0)$ at $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ respectively. Hence $B(1)\otimes B(1)=B(2)\sqcup B(0)$, matching the classical decomposition $V(1)\otimes V(1)=V(2)\oplus V(0)$ of dimensions $3=2+1$; here $B(2)$ is the three-element $1$-chain of weights $2\lambda_1,0,-2\lambda_1$ and $B(0)$ the one-element crystal of weight $0$.
items.strategy:
Direct computation with the two-case rule, cross-checked against the rank-one described crystals.

1.1 Read off the four residues and the values $\varepsilon_1(v_0)=0,\varphi_1(v_0)=1,\varepsilon_1(v_1)=1,\varphi_1(v_1)=0$ from the two-element chain $v_0\xrightarrow{1}v_1$, which is the $m=1$ case of the rank-one crystal basis of [[thm-quantized-sl-two-string-formulas]] with divided powers ($[0]_1!$ conventions of [[def-quantum-integers-factorials-and-divided-powers-at-q-i]]). [given]

2.1 Apply the rule vertex by vertex: $\tilde f_1(v_0\otimes v_0)=v_1\otimes v_0$ since $1>0$; $\tilde f_1(v_1\otimes v_0)=v_1\otimes v_1$ since $0\le0$; $\tilde f_1(v_1\otimes v_1)=0$ since $\tilde f_1v_1=0$ and $0\le1$; $\tilde f_1(v_0\otimes v_1)=0$ since $1\le1$ selects the second factor and $\tilde f_1v_1=0$. This gives the two components stated, with the highest vertices $v_0\otimes v_0$ and $v_0\otimes v_1$. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Compute $\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1$ by iterating the same rule and compare with the max formulas of [[lem-crystal-tensor-product-weight-epsilon-and-phi-formulas]], using $\langle h_1,wt(v_0)\rangle=1$ and $\langle h_1,wt(v_1)\rangle=-1$: at $v_0\otimes v_0$, $\varepsilon_1=\max(0,0-1)=0$ and $\varphi_1=\max(\varphi_1(v_0)+\langle h_1,wt(v_0)\rangle,\varphi_1(v_0))=\max(1+1,1)=2$; at $v_1\otimes v_0$, $\varepsilon_1=\max(1,0-(-1))=1$ and $\varphi_1=\max(0+1,1)=1$; at $v_1\otimes v_1$, $\varepsilon_1=\max(1,1-(-1))=2$ and $\varphi_1=\max(0-1,0)=0$; at $v_0\otimes v_1$, $\varepsilon_1=\max(0,1-1)=0$ and $\varphi_1=\max(1-1,0)=0$. [step 2.1, step 1.1]

4.1 Identify the components. The three-element chain has top weight $2\lambda_1$, middle weight $0$, bottom weight $-2\lambda_1$ and one colour; a connected crystal with a unique highest vertex of weight $2\lambda_1$ and $\varphi_1+\varepsilon_1+1=3$ vertices in its only string is the rank-one crystal $B(2)$ of [[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]] (the $m=2$ case of the same rank-one description). The remaining vertex is fixed by both operators and has weight $0$, so it is $B(0)$. This identifies the two components without invoking the general uniqueness theorem, so the example is choice-free. [step 3.1, step 2.1]

5.1 Cross-check the count: the components have $3$ and $1$ vertices, and $V(1)\otimes V(1)\cong V(2)\oplus V(0)$ because the highest vector $v_0\otimes v_0$ generates a copy of $V(2)$ and the orthogonal complement is one dimensional of weight $0$; the crystal dimensions equal the module dimensions by [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. [step 4.1, step 2.1] ∎

items.title: Highest components in the $A_2$ tensor crystal $B(\lambda_1)\otimes B(\lambda_1)$
items.statement:
Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3$ with simple roots $\alpha_1=2\lambda_1-\lambda_2$, $\alpha_2=-\lambda_1+2\lambda_2$ and $\langle h_i,\lambda_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}$. The three-dimensional simple module $V(\lambda_1)$ has crystal $B(\lambda_1)=\{u_1,u_2,u_3\}$ with weights $\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2-\lambda_1,\ -\lambda_2$ and arrows $u_1\xrightarrow{1}u_2\xrightarrow{2}u_3$; its only nonzero $\varepsilon$-values are $\varepsilon_1(u_2)=1,\ \varepsilon_2(u_3)=1$, and $\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,wt(b)\rangle$.

In the tensor crystal $B(\lambda_1)\otimes B(\lambda_1)$ of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] the criterion of [[thm-highest-weight-components-in-a-tensor-product-crystal]](a) applies. A vertex $b_1\otimes b_2$ is highest exactly when $\varepsilon_i(b_1)=0$ for $i=1,2$ and $\varepsilon_i(b_2)\le\langle h_i,wt(b_1)\rangle$ for $i=1,2$. Since $\varepsilon_1(u_2)=1$ and $\varepsilon_2(u_3)=1$, only $b_1=u_1$ can occur, so the highest vertices are
$$u_1\otimes u_1\quad(\text{weight }2\lambda_1),\qquad u_1\otimes u_2\quad(\text{weight }\lambda_2),$$
the second because $\varepsilon_1(u_2)=1\le\langle h_1,wt(u_1)\rangle=1$ and $\varepsilon_2(u_2)=0\le\langle h_2,wt(u_1)\rangle=0$, while $u_1\otimes u_3$ fails since $\varepsilon_2(u_3)=1>\langle h_2,wt(u_1)\rangle=0$. By [[thm-highest-weight-components-in-a-tensor-product-crystal]](b) the two generated components are the highest weight crystals $B(2\lambda_1)$ and $B(\lambda_2)$, so the nine vertices split as $B(\lambda_1)\otimes B(\lambda_1)=B(2\lambda_1)\sqcup B(\lambda_2)$, matching $V(\lambda_1)\otimes V(\lambda_1)=V(2\lambda_1)\oplus V(\lambda_2)$ with dimensions $9=6+3$.
items.strategy:
The criterion computation and a direct component count, cross-checked against the classical decomposition.

1.1 Compute $\varepsilon_i$ of the three standard vertices from the arrows of $B(\lambda_1)$ read as a crystal of the standard module: $\tilde e_1u_2=u_1$, $\tilde e_1u_1=0$, $\tilde e_1u_3=0$ and $\tilde e_2u_3=u_2$, $\tilde e_2u_2=\tilde e_2u_1=0$, so $\varepsilon_1=(0,1,0)$ and $\varepsilon_2=(0,0,1)$ at $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$; the weights are $\lambda_1,\lambda_2-\lambda_1,-\lambda_2$ as stated. [given]

2.1 Apply the highest-vertex criterion of [[thm-highest-weight-components-in-a-tensor-product-crystal]](a): $\varepsilon_1(b_1)=0$ forces $b_1\ne u_2$ and $\varepsilon_2(b_1)=0$ forces $b_1\ne u_3$, so $b_1=u_1$; then $\varepsilon_1(b_2)\le1$ always holds and $\varepsilon_2(b_2)\le0$ forces $b_2\ne u_3$. Hence the highest vertices are $u_1\otimes u_1$ and $u_1\otimes u_2$, of weights $2\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_1+(\lambda_2-\lambda_1)=\lambda_2$, both dominant. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Verify by the two-case rule that $u_1\otimes u_3$ is not highest: $\varphi_2(u_1)=\langle h_2,wt(u_1)\rangle=0<1=\varepsilon_2(u_3)$, so $\tilde e_2$ acts on the second factor and $\tilde e_2(u_1\otimes u_3)=u_1\otimes u_2\ne0$. [step 1.1, algebra]

4.1 By [[thm-highest-weight-components-in-a-tensor-product-crystal]](b) the component of $u_1\otimes u_1$ is isomorphic to $B(2\lambda_1)$ and that of $u_1\otimes u_2$ to $B(\lambda_2)$; since the theorem identifies the components of the tensor crystal with the simple constituents of $V(\lambda_1)\otimes V(\lambda_1)$ and $9=6+3$, the two components exhaust the nine vertices. [step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 Cross-check with the source computation: the tensor square of the standard representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ decomposes as $V(2\lambda_1)\oplus V(\lambda_2)$ (symmetric square plus exterior square), and the two highest vertices found are exactly the highest vectors of these summands; this is the computation drawn in the source. [step 4.1]

5.2 Choice: clause (a) of the criterion is a finite computation; the identification in step 4.1 uses the uniqueness theorem, whose axiom of choice is declared in this item through [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used only as in its own contract. [step 4.1, given] ∎

items.title: Dual crystals reverse arrows and weights: two small computations
items.statement:
The example computes the dual crystal of [[prop-dual-crystal-and-reversal-conventions]] in two small cases.

(A) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, let $B(1)=\{v_0\xrightarrow{1}v_1\}$ with $wt(v_0)=\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1)=-\lambda_1$ and $\varepsilon_1(v_0)=0,\varphi_1(v_0)=1,\varepsilon_1(v_1)=1,\varphi_1(v_1)=0$ (as in [[ex-tensor-crystal-b-one-tensor-b-one-for-sl-two]]). Then $B(1)^\vee=\{v_0^\vee,v_1^\vee\}$ has the single arrow $v_1^\vee\xrightarrow{1}v_0^\vee$, weights $wt(v_0^\vee)=-\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1^\vee)=\lambda_1$, and $(\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1)$ equal to $(1,0)$ at $v_0^\vee$ and $(0,1)$ at $v_1^\vee$. Hence $B(1)^\vee\cong B(1)$ as crystals, realized with the highest vertex $v_1^\vee$.

(B) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3$, let $B(\lambda_1)=\{u_1\xrightarrow{1}u_2\xrightarrow{2}u_3\}$ be the standard crystal of [[ex-highest-components-in-a-small-type-a-two-tensor-crystal]].
